# Exercise 2.3 — Transforming {#sec-transforming}


## Objectives

::: {.objective-list}
- Measure the skewness of a variable and say, from the number alone, roughly
  what its histogram looks like.
- Apply min-max scaling, standardisation and a log transformation, and state
  for each one what it changes and what it leaves alone.
- Say which of the three you would apply before fitting a linear model, and
  why the honest answer is "it depends on the model".
:::

## Why this, here

@sec-correlation-missing left you with a complete table of numbers. Models are
sensitive to the *scale* and the *shape* of those numbers in ways that have
nothing to do with the clinical content: a variable measured in thousands
dominates one measured in units, and a long right tail puts most of the
leverage in a handful of patients. This exercise is about what the common fixes
actually do — including the one that does nothing.

## A third file, and a warning about its last column

`data/bupa.csv` holds 345 patients with five liver-related blood tests (`mcv`,
`alkalinephosphotase`, `alamine`, `aspartate`, `gammaGlut`), a count of daily
alcoholic `drinks`, and a column called `selector`. There are no missing
values.

::: {.callout-warning}
## `selector` is not a diagnosis
It is the field the original depositors used to split the file into two sets,
200 rows and 145 rows. Tutorials across the internet model it as a liver
disease label; it is not one, and a model that predicts it is predicting an
arbitrary partition. We use this file only for transformation, where the label
plays no part.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
library(readr); library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(ggplot2)
bupa <- read_csv("data/bupa.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
dim(bupa)
summary(bupa)
```

## Python

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
bupa = pd.read_csv("data/bupa.csv")
print(bupa.shape)
bupa.describe().round(2)
```
:::

Compare the mean and the median of `gammaGlut`, then of `mcv`. In one of them
they agree; in the other the mean is half as large again as the median. That
gap is the fingerprint of a right tail, and skewness puts a number on it.

$$g_1 = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^3}{\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2\right]^{3/2}}$$

Zero for a symmetric variable, positive when the tail is to the right. Above
about 1 it is worth doing something about; above 2 the mean is no longer a
useful summary. This is one formula, not two: R has no `skewness()` in base, so
we write it, and pandas has `.skew()` built in with a small-sample correction
that makes no visible difference at this size.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
skewness <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  mean((x - mean(x))^3) / mean((x - mean(x))^2)^1.5
}
labs_cols <- c("mcv", "alkalinephosphotase", "alamine", "aspartate", "gammaGlut", "drinks")
sapply(bupa[labs_cols], skewness) |> round(2)
```

## Python

```{python}
labs_cols = ["mcv", "alkalinephosphotase", "alamine", "aspartate", "gammaGlut", "drinks"]
bupa[labs_cols].skew().round(2)
```
:::

`alamine`, `gammaGlut` and `aspartate` are strongly right-skewed, around 3.1,
2.9 and 2.3. `mcv` is mildly left-skewed. Plot the two extremes and the numbers
become a picture.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
bupa |>
  select(mcv, gammaGlut) |>
  pivot_longer(everything()) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  facet_wrap(~ name, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Patients")
```

## Python

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.2))
for ax, col in zip(axes, ["mcv", "gammaGlut"]):
    ax.hist(bupa[col], bins=30)
    ax.set_title(col)
    ax.set_xlabel(None); ax.set_ylabel("Patients")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

## Three transformations

| Transformation | Formula | Range after | Shape after |
|---|---|---|---|
| Min-max scaling | $(x - \min) / (\max - \min)$ | $[0, 1]$ | unchanged |
| Standardisation (z-score) | $(x - \mu) / \sigma$ | mean 0, sd 1 | unchanged |
| Log | $\log(x)$ | depends | compressed on the right |

: {tbl-colwidths="[28,28,22,22]"}

The third column is what everyone remembers and the fourth is what matters.
Here are all three applied to `gammaGlut`.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
g <- bupa$gammaGlut
transformed <- tibble(
  raw     = g,
  minmax  = (g - min(g)) / (max(g) - min(g)),
  zscore  = (g - mean(g)) / sd(g),
  logged  = log(g)
)
sapply(transformed, skewness) |> round(2)
sapply(transformed, function(x) c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x))) |> round(2)
```

## Python

```{python}
from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler, StandardScaler

g = bupa[["gammaGlut"]]
transformed = pd.DataFrame({
    "raw":    g["gammaGlut"],
    "minmax": MinMaxScaler().fit_transform(g).ravel(),
    "zscore": StandardScaler().fit_transform(g).ravel(),
    "logged": np.log(g["gammaGlut"]),
})
print(transformed.skew().round(2))
print(transformed.agg(["mean", "std"]).round(2))
```
:::

## The result that should bother you

Min-max scaling and standardisation leave the skewness **exactly** where it
was. Only the log moves it, from about 2.9 to about 0.5.

1. Both scalings are *affine*: they multiply by one constant and subtract
   another. Skewness is built from the ratio of the third and second central
   moments, and that ratio is unchanged by multiplication — the constant
   cancels, top and bottom. The number is identical, not approximately
   identical.
2. So "normalising" the data does not make it normal. It makes it *comparable*,
   which is a different problem, solved for a different reason: a distance, a
   penalty or a gradient step treats a variable in thousands differently from
   one in units.
3. The log is the only one of the three that changes the shape, because it is
   not affine. It also changes the meaning: a coefficient fitted to
   `log(gammaGlut)` is about proportional change, not absolute, and that is
   something you have to be willing to say in the discussion section.

See it rather than take it on trust: three boxplots of the same variable.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
transformed |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "transform") |>
  mutate(transform = factor(transform, levels = c("raw", "minmax", "zscore", "logged"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = transform, y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ transform, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

## Python

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(9, 3))
for ax, col in zip(axes, transformed.columns):
    ax.boxplot(transformed[col])
    ax.set_title(col); ax.set_xticks([])
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

The first three boxes are the same picture with different numbers on the axis.
The fourth is a different picture.

## Task 1 — The original's question, with the trap left in

This was the task on the page this exercise comes from, and it is a good one.

> 1.1 Load the bupa dataset and apply a transformation of your choice to a
> feature of your choice.
> 1.2 Remove the label column (`selector`) from the dataset.
> 1.3 Visualise the data before and after the transformation using boxplots.

Do it — and when you reach 1.2, write one sentence saying why that step is in
the list. It is not because `selector` is a label you must protect from
leaking. It is because it is not a label at all, and a boxplot of it would
invite you to treat it as one.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
bupa_labs <- bupa |> select(-______)

bupa_logged <- bupa_labs |> mutate(across(c(alamine, aspartate, gammaGlut), ______))

sk <- sapply(bupa_logged[c("alamine", "aspartate", "gammaGlut")], skewness)
sk
max(sk)   # expect -1 to 1
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
`select()` drops a column when you put a minus in front of its name. For the
transformation, the function is `log` — pass it as a bare function name inside
`across()`, not as a call.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
bupa_labs <- bupa |> select(-selector)

bupa_logged <- bupa_labs |> mutate(across(c(alamine, aspartate, gammaGlut), log))

sk <- sapply(bupa_logged[c("alamine", "aspartate", "gammaGlut")], skewness)
sk
max(sk)   # expect -1 to 1

bind_rows(before = bupa_labs, after = bupa_logged, .id = "state") |>
  pivot_longer(c(alamine, aspartate, gammaGlut)) |>
  mutate(state = factor(state, levels = c("before", "after"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = name, y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ state, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
skewed = ["alamine", "aspartate", "gammaGlut"]
bupa_labs = bupa.drop(columns=["______"])

bupa_logged = bupa_labs.copy()
bupa_logged[skewed] = np.______(bupa_labs[skewed])

sk = bupa_logged[skewed].skew()
print(sk)
print(sk.max())   # expect -1 to 1
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
skewed = ["alamine", "aspartate", "gammaGlut"]
bupa_labs = bupa.drop(columns=["selector"])

bupa_logged = bupa_labs.copy()
bupa_logged[skewed] = np.log(bupa_labs[skewed])

sk = bupa_logged[skewed].skew()
print(sk)
print(sk.max())   # expect -1 to 1

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.2))
bupa_labs[skewed].plot.box(ax=axes[0], title="before")
bupa_logged[skewed].plot.box(ax=axes[1], title="after")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::
:::
:::

## Task 2 — Where the log is not available

`drinks` is right-skewed too, and nine patients report zero. `log(0)` is
`-Inf`, which propagates into every summary and plot downstream.

Try `log(drinks)` first and look at what you get. Then use `log1p()`, which
computes $\log(1 + x)$, and compare the skewness of both against the raw
column.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
sum(bupa$drinks == 0)
summary(log(bupa$drinks))              # look before you fix

drinks_log1p <- ______(bupa$drinks)
c(raw = skewness(bupa$drinks), log1p = skewness(drinks_log1p))
skewness(drinks_log1p)   # expect -1 to 1
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
sum(bupa$drinks == 0)
summary(log(bupa$drinks))              # look before you fix

drinks_log1p <- log1p(bupa$drinks)
c(raw = skewness(bupa$drinks), log1p = skewness(drinks_log1p))
skewness(drinks_log1p)   # expect -1 to 1
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
print((bupa["drinks"] == 0).sum())
print(np.log(bupa["drinks"]).describe())    # look before you fix

drinks_log1p = np.______(bupa["drinks"])
print(bupa["drinks"].skew(), drinks_log1p.skew())
print(drinks_log1p.skew())   # expect -1 to 1
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
print((bupa["drinks"] == 0).sum())
print(np.log(bupa["drinks"]).describe())    # look before you fix

drinks_log1p = np.log1p(bupa["drinks"])
print(bupa["drinks"].skew(), drinks_log1p.skew())
print(drinks_log1p.skew())   # expect -1 to 1
```
:::
:::
:::

Adding 1 is a choice, not a fact. It is defensible for a count of drinks, where
the units are fixed and 1 is small; it is arbitrary for a laboratory value in
mu U/ml, where the same "+1" means something different depending on the assay.
Say which you did.

## Reflection

1. A colleague standardises every predictor before fitting a linear regression
   and reports that the model improved. What do you suspect happened, and what
   would you ask to see?
2. You log-transform `gammaGlut` and fit a model. A hepatologist asks what the
   coefficient means. Answer in one sentence, in their units, not yours.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Expected values.** Skewness: `alamine` 3.0–3.1, `gammaGlut` 2.8–2.9,
`aspartate` 2.2–2.3, `drinks` 1.5, `mcv` about −0.4. After `log`: all three
skewed labs fall to between 0.3 and 0.6. `log1p(drinks)` lands near 0.1.
Min-max and z-score skewness are identical to the raw value to every printed
digit — if a student reports otherwise, they have transformed a different
column.

**Reflection 1.** Standardisation cannot change the fit of an ordinary linear
regression at all: the predictions, residuals and $R^2$ are identical, and only
the coefficients are rescaled. So either the "improvement" is in the
interpretability of the coefficients, or something else changed at the same
time — a dropped row, a different split, or a penalised model, where
standardisation genuinely does change the answer because the penalty acts on
the coefficient scale. Ask to see both fits.

**Reflection 2.** With `log` base e, a coefficient of $\beta$ means that a
doubling of gammaGlut is associated with $\beta \log 2$ units of outcome; the
clinically sayable version is "per doubling", not "per unit of log".

**Common failures.** (1) `across(..., log())` with the parentheses, which
evaluates `log()` with no argument. (2) Students concluding that min-max
scaling "fixed" the skew because the axis numbers got smaller — go back to the
boxplot panel, which is why it is four panels and not one. (3) Someone will
model `selector`. Let them, then ask what the two groups are.

**Timing.** Forty minutes is enough if the three transformations are presented
from the front and the class only does Tasks 1 and 2. The skewness formula
rewards five minutes at the whiteboard for anyone who has not met moments.
:::
:::

## Stretch

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 1 — Is `selector` really arbitrary?
Compare `gammaGlut` between the two `selector` groups. The means differ by more
than you might expect of a random partition — which does not make it a
diagnosis, but does mean the split was not made by shuffling. What would you
need to know before using either group on its own?
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 2 — Transformations that are fitted
`log()` needs nothing from the data: the same input always gives the same
output. Min-max needs a minimum and a maximum; standardisation needs a mean and
a standard deviation; the Box-Cox transformation estimates a power. Sort the
four into those that are *fitted* and those that are not, and keep the list —
in @sec-leakage, it is exactly the fitted ones that have to be learned on the
training set alone.
:::

## What you can and cannot now claim

**Can:** that you can measure skewness, name what each of three transformations
changes, and demonstrate that two of them do not change shape at all.

**Cannot:** that you have applied any of them safely. Every transformation in
this chapter was fitted to all 345 rows at once, including the rows you would
have held back for testing. @sec-leakage is about what that costs.
